title: Variable-size window
sub: Grow on the right, shrink on the left: why a nested while is still O(n), and when the window breaks
cards/0/title: The problem and the key property
cards/0/body:
Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters (LeetCode #3). Given a string s, find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters. Constraints: 0 ≤ |s| ≤ 5·10⁴; the string contains English letters, digits, symbols and spaces.

Examples: "abcabcbb" → 3 (“abc”), "bbbbb" → 1, "pwwkew" → 3 (“wke”). “pwke” does not count: it is a subsequence, the letters are taken with a gap.

The signals are the same as for a fixed-size window — a contiguous piece and the best one — but the length is not given; it is what we are looking for. A variable-size window works when the condition is monotonic:

— if a window is valid, every window inside it is valid too: removing a character cannot add a repeat;
— if a window is invalid, every window containing it is invalid too: the repeat does not go away.

Hence the strategy: once the window breaks, growing it is pointless — shrink from the left. While the window is valid, try to grow it.
cards/1/q: Substring s[l..r] has no repeats. What can you say about s[l+1..r] and about s[l..r+1]?
cards/1/options/0: s[l+1..r] definitely has no repeats; s[l..r+1] depends on the character s[r+1]
cards/1/options/2: s[l+1..r] may contain a repeat, while s[l..r+1] cannot
cards/1/explain: Removing a character on the left cannot create more repeats. Adding one on the right creates a repeat if s[r+1] is already inside. That is monotonicity: a valid window stays valid after shrinking, and an invalid one stays invalid after growing. That is why the left edge only ever moves forward.
cards/1/wrong/1: Growing can break the window: “abc” has no repeats, but “abca” does.
cards/1/wrong/2: The other way round: removing a character from a repeat-free window cannot produce a repeat. Adding one can.
cards/2/title: From brute force to a window
cards/2/body:
Brute force: from every start i, walk right with a HashSet<char> until a repeat shows up. For an arbitrary alphabet that is O(n²). A fair caveat: a repeat-free substring is no longer than the alphabet size σ, so here brute force is O(n·σ), and on LeetCode with σ ≈ 95 it even passes. But for integers or Unicode it is a square, and the interviewer expects O(n).

What is repeated: brute force hits a repeat at j and restarts from i + 1 — re-checking characters i+1..j−1 that are already known to be distinct. Don’t reset the window: the right edge r only moves forward, and when s[r] is already inside, move the left edge l until the duplicate is gone.

Invariant: after the inner while, the window s[l..r] has no repeats — and that is when the answer is updated.

Why O(n) despite the while. Count not one iteration of the for but all the work in the pass. Each Remove moves l by one, and l only grows and cannot overtake r. So over the whole pass there are at most n removals and exactly n additions — at most 2n set operations. A single iteration can be expensive (four removals in a row), but the total is linear.
cards/3/q: How many times in total does the while body — window.Remove(s[l++]) — run over a whole pass on a string of length n?
cards/3/options/0: At most n: each character is removed from the window at most once
cards/3/options/1: Up to n on every iteration of the for — up to n² in total
cards/3/options/2: Exactly as many times as there are repeated characters in the string
cards/3/explain: Each removal moves l by one, l only grows and never overtakes r. So over the whole pass there are at most n removals, and at most 2n set operations in total. That is “amortised O(1) per step”: the expensive iterations are rare and paid for by the cheap ones.
cards/3/wrong/1: That would be the case if l were reset backwards. But l only grows: a removed character never re-enters from the same position.
cards/3/wrong/2: In “gamedev” one letter repeats, yet there are four removals: g, a, m and the first e. Everything to the left of the duplicate goes.
cards/4/task: Step through the trace on "gamedev". The rig stops when the second “e” arrives at the window “gamed” and asks what the code does.
cards/4/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: Removes the first “e” from the middle of the window
cards/4/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: Restarts the window at the new “e”: l = 5
cards/4/goal/asks/0/q: Window “gamed”, an “e” arrives, and an “e” is already inside. What does the code do?
cards/4/goal/asks/0/explain: A window is a contiguous piece; you cannot cut out the middle. For the first “e” (index 3) to leave, everything to its left leaves too: g, a, m and the e itself — four iterations of the while. Restarting at l = 5 would lose the “d”: the window “de” has no repeats and must not be thrown away.
cards/5/body:
Four removals one by one can be replaced by one jump. Remember, for every character, where it was seen last. If s[r] was already at position p inside the window, the left edge jumps straight to p + 1.

The subtlety: a character’s last position may be left of the window — the character left long ago. Then l must not move. Hence l = Math.Max(l, …): the left edge never moves backwards.

A handy trick is to store index + 1: a fresh array is all zeros, and zero itself means “not seen”, so there is no need to fill it with −1. 128 slots are enough because the problem guarantees ASCII characters.

The complexity is the same, O(n), but now every step is O(1) with no amortisation and no hashing. Memory is O(σ).
cards/5/deep:
Why the jump loses nothing. Let s[r] = c with the previous c at p ≥ l. Every window that starts in l..p and ends at r or later contains both cs — it is invalid. So the starts l..p can be discarded at once for all future r. It is the same discard argument as for converging pointers.

Unicode. A .NET char is a UTF-16 code unit from 0 to 65,535. For arbitrary text an int[65536] is 256 KB per call; a Dictionary<char, int> is better then. And what a person calls a character can be two chars: an emoji outside the Basic Multilingual Plane is a surrogate pair. If the interviewer says “character” about such text, ask whether to count code units or code points; for the latter .NET Core 3.0+ has System.Text.Rune and string.EnumerateRunes(), which Unity does not have.

No allocations. Span<int> next = stackalloc int[128]; is 512 bytes on the stack instead of an array on the heap. C# zeroes stackalloc memory by default (unless [SkipLocalsInit] is applied), so the “zero means not seen” trick still works. Unity has Span<T> since 2021.2 (.NET Standard 2.1). The HashSet<char> version is several times slower: a hash and a bucket lookup on every operation, plus allocating the set itself.
cards/6/q: On the string "abba" this code returns 3, but the right answer is 2. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/6/explain: At r = 2 the second “b” sets l = 2. At r = 3 an “a” arrives, its previous position is 0, and the code sets l = 1: the left edge jumps back into the window “bba”, which has a repeat, length 3. The earlier “a” is already outside the window and l must not move. The fix is the invariant “l never decreases”: l = Math.Max(l, next[c]).
cards/7/title: The mirror template: the shortest window
cards/7/body:
Minimum Size Subarray Sum (LeetCode #209). Given an array of positive integers nums and a number target, find the minimal length of a contiguous subarray with sum ≥ target, or 0 if there is none. Constraints: 1 ≤ target ≤ 10⁹, 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵, 1 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁴.

The monotonicity is mirrored here: the numbers are positive, so a valid window (sum ≥ target) stays valid when it grows, and shrinking only lowers the sum. Once you find a valid window, growing it further is pointless — anything longer is valid anyway. Record the length and shrink, trying to make it shorter.

Two templates worth telling apart out loud:
— looking for the longest — shrink while the window is bad, take the answer after the while;
— looking for the shortest — shrink while the window is good, take the answer inside the while.

The complexity is the same, O(n): l only grows. The sum is at most 10⁵·10⁴ = 10⁹ and fits in an int. If no window is valid, best stays int.MaxValue — that must be turned into 0.
cards/7/deep:
The LeetCode follow-up: O(n log n). Prefix sums of positive numbers are strictly increasing. For each start i, binary-search the first j with prefix[j] − prefix[i] ≥ target — Array.BinarySearch over the prefix array (when the value is absent it returns ~index of the insertion point). It is worse than the window, but it shows you see the monotonicity of prefixes. The window is O(n) time and O(1) memory.

Why positivity matters so much. The window proof relies on the fact that for a fixed r the sum of [l..r] decreases as l grows. With zeros it does not increase — the window still works. With negative numbers the property is gone and you need a different tool: prefixes and a monotonic deque (LeetCode #862, lesson 4).
cards/8/q: Assemble the Minimum Size Subarray Sum solution.
cards/8/explain: We want the shortest, so shrink while the window is good: while (sum >= target), and record the length r − l + 1 inside. nums[l++] subtracts the current left element and only then moves the edge; nums[++l] would subtract its neighbour. If no window was valid, best is still int.MaxValue, and the problem says to return 0.
cards/9/task: Step through the trace on [1, 4, 2, 5, 1, 1, 3, 6], target = 8. The rig stops after the first shrink and asks what to do next.
cards/9/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: Shrink again: record length 3 and drop the 4
cards/9/goal/asks/0/q: Length 4 was recorded and the 1 dropped on the left: window [4, 2, 5], sum = 11. What next?
cards/9/goal/asks/0/explain: 11 ≥ 8 — the window [4, 2, 5] is still good, so the while goes on: record length 3 and drop the 4, sum = 7. Growing a good window is pointless — every extension is good too, just longer. And it is too early to stop: [3, 6] of length 2 is still ahead.
cards/10/title: When the window does not work
cards/10/body:
Everything rests on monotonicity. With negative numbers it breaks: shrinking can increase the sum, and growing can decrease it.

Example: nums = [1, −1, 5], target = 5. The window reaches r = 2 with sum 5, records length 3, drops the 1, the sum becomes 4 < 5, and the while stops. The window concludes that nothing shorter exists and returns 3. But the answer is 1: the subarray [5]. Reaching it required dropping the −1 as well, which would have increased the sum — the window never considers that.

What to use instead:
— “sum exactly k, numbers of any sign” (LeetCode #560) — prefix sums in a dictionary: the sum of [l..r] is prefix[r+1] − prefix[l], and at each step you look up how many times the prefix prefix − k has occurred. That is the prefix sums lesson in the hash map unit;
— “shortest with sum ≥ k, numbers of any sign” (LeetCode #862) — prefixes plus a monotonic deque, lesson 4 of this unit.

Zeros don’t break monotonicity: with them the sum does not grow when you shrink, and the window works.
cards/11/q: Where does a variable-size window give the right answer in O(n)? Select all.
cards/11/options/0: The longest subarray with at most two distinct numbers
cards/11/options/1: The shortest subarray with sum ≥ target, all numbers positive
cards/11/options/2: The shortest subarray with sum ≥ target, numbers of any sign
cards/11/options/3: How many subarrays sum to exactly k, numbers of any sign
cards/11/options/4: The longest substring where each letter occurs at most twice
cards/11/explain: “At most two distinct” and “each letter at most twice” are monotonic: the condition holds inside a valid window, and growing an invalid one does not fix it. Positive numbers are the “shortest” template. With negative numbers shrinking can increase the sum, so there is no monotonicity: “≥ target” needs prefixes and a deque, “exactly k” needs prefixes in a dictionary.
cards/12/q: You are solving Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters out loud. Put the steps in order.
cards/12/items/0: Clarify: substring, not subsequence; which characters — ASCII or any Unicode; the empty string
cards/12/items/1: Name the brute force: from every start walk to the first repeat — O(n²) for a large alphabet
cards/12/items/2: Idea: a repeat-free window, grow on the right, shrink on the left on a repeat — the left edge never goes back
cards/12/items/3: Write the code, saying the invariant out loud: s[l..r] has no repeats, l only grows
cards/12/items/4: Run "abba": check that l does not jump backwards
cards/12/items/5: State the complexity: O(n) time, O(σ) memory — and why the while does not make it quadratic
cards/12/items/6: Edge cases: empty string, all characters equal, all distinct
cards/12/explain: Statement, baseline, idea, code with the invariant, a run, complexity, edge cases. “abba” is the best example to run: it breaks the jump without Math.Max. And interviewers often ask separately why the nested while is still O(n).
